item.title: Former Southern University professor tied to Nobel Prize-winning discovery
item.description: Southern University and A&M College professor emeritus Ali R. Fazely, Ph.D. has contributed to research connected to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the groundbreaking scientific project at the center of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. Fazely collaborated with Francis Halzen, Ph.D., a University of Wisconsin–Madison physicist who received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. The American Institute of Physics announced the recognition Oct. 6. Located at the South Pole, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory uses more than 5,000 optical sensors embedded in approximately one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice to detect faint flashes of light produced when neutrinos interact with matter. These nearly massless particles can travel vast distances through the universe, carrying information about some of its most energetic events. The discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources gave scientists a new way to study distant cosmic events beyond traditional observations using light. Fazely has led Southern’s IceCube-related research activities since 1997, working with graduate students, post-doctoral researchers and scientific collaborators. His team’s work has focused on detector simulations, rare particle decays, supernova neutrinos and high-energy neutrino interaction cross sections. Fazely said Southern’s participation in the international collaboration highlights the role historically Black colleges and universities can play in advancing scientific research. “Southern University's participation demonstrates that HBCUs can be active contributors to these efforts, not simply observers of discoveries made elsewhere,” said Fazely. Southern’s research has helped support the scientific work behind the observatory through computer simulations that model how neutrinos interact with matter, how charged particles travel through ice and how light reaches the detector’s optical sensors. These models help researchers interpret the signals IceCube records, reconstruct neutrino energies and directions, and assess potential improvements to the detector. The university’s research group has developed simulations for the existing IceCube detector, the IceCube Upgrade and the proposed IceCube-Gen2 observatory. Recent efforts have focused on supernova-neutrino simulations and future detector configurations that could help scientists identify astrophysical signals and investigate physical processes that have not yet been observed. Fazely’s research also includes studies of rare particle decays and high-energy neutrino interactions. A study exploring the possibility of observing the rare decay of an eta particle into a neutrino-antineutrino pair was published in Physical Review D in 2010. In 2019, the team published research in Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics introducing a Prime-Index parametrization of neutrino-nucleon and proton-proton cross sections. The research program has also created opportunities for Southern students to participate in advanced scientific investigations. Fazely said two students, Cheng Guo and Aaron Richard, completed Master of Science degrees through IceCube-related research, while graduate student Justin Mitchell is currently involved in the program. Through their involvement, students gain experience in particle physics, astrophysics, computer programming, statistical analysis and large-scale scientific simulations. They also become familiar with the research methods and scientific standards used in major international collaborations, preparing them for doctoral studies, research careers, national laboratories and technology-related professions. For Fazely, the program’s impact extends beyond scientific findings to the development of future researchers. “I am particularly proud that our program has combined scientific research with the education and mentoring of young scientists," he said. "In my view, that is one of Southern University's most important contributions to the future of physics.”

item.title: Southern University System Presidential Search Committee announces finalists for system president
Southern University students create award-winning platform to support cancer patients
item.description: Courtesy of Nexus Louisiana Competing in DevDays for the first time, the team won with Tomorrow, a platform that helps patients protect their emotional well-being and sense of identity during treatment When a Southern University business professor forwarded Jha'Hannah Pink an email about DevDays, the timing was personal. Pink, an agribusiness major, had recently lost her uncle to cancer. He became the motivation behind Tomorrow, the cancer support platform she and her teammates built during the 10-week competition. Tomorrow won first place in the DevDays Cancer Care and Prevention Challenge in Southern University's first time competing in DevDays. The competition is a partnership between Nexus Louisiana and Ochsner Health that asked Louisiana college students to build technology to improve the cancer care experience for patients, caregivers and healthcare teams. "Tomorrow is about giving patients a reason to look forward to tomorrow," Pink said. "A lot of times, when you have all those treatments and appointments, you forget what you're living for and who you're living for. Our app is centered around helping patients remember that and helping them fight for tomorrow." Pink and her teammates, Thomas Reid and Jalayah Jones, study business and nursing. They earned $6,000 for the win. A platform built around quality of life Tomorrow is designed to work alongside hospital care. It helps patients keep their sense of identity, look after their emotional well-being and stay connected to the people and experiences that matter most during treatment. "I think healthcare does a good job at keeping them alive, but who is helping them harness that life inside of them, keep them positive, keep them happy?" Pink said. Patients get a personal profile where they can track their emotional wellness with hopeScore. They also receive encouraging reminders through tomorrowSpark and have access to an appointment calendar and AI-powered guidance. The platform includes Living Proof, a collection of survivor stories, along with wellness resources, cancer news and research, and a Legacy Vault where patients can save memories and life stories. The goal is to put quality of life alongside treatment, so patients remember not only what they are fighting against, but what they are fighting for. Building the app was the team's biggest hurdle. "We are not in computer science, so it was difficult trying to find a platform that incorporated everything that I wanted to have in it," Pink said. For Pink, the most valuable part of the experience was finally presenting the team's work to the judges. "I feel relieved. I'm happy," she said. "I think the judges and everyone kind of saw the vision." Multiple approaches to one challenge About 50 students from nine colleges and universities applied to compete in the challenge. Ten teams advanced to the finals, representing Southern University, Southeastern Louisiana University, the Edward Via College of Osteopathic Medicine, the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, the University of Louisiana at Monroe and Louisiana Tech University. Finalist teams presented their prototypes on Sept. 25 at Nexus Louisiana's Baton Rouge headquarters to a panel of healthcare, technology and business leaders. They competed for a share of $10,000 in cash prizes. Second place and $3,000 went to OncoReady from the University of Louisiana at Monroe. Computer science and engineering students Pankaj Bhatta, Jeevan Parajuli and Swabhiman Paudel developed a prototype to help care teams identify and address clinical and logistical barriers before a patient's scheduled cancer treatment. Third place and $1,000 went to Cancer Krewe from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. Computer science and engineering students Kaitlyn Damare, Ky Smith and Amaya Erhabor built a caregiver and treatment coordination web app that helps patients and their support circles organize appointments, delegate tasks and understand medical information. "Each team approached the same problem differently, showing the many ways technology can support patients and families," said Tony Zanders, president and CEO of Nexus Louisiana. "Tomorrow shows what can happen when students bring their personal experiences and skills to a real challenge. This is not just a project. There are real lives impacted by this technology." Ten weeks of development Over 10 weeks, student teams developed solutions focused on patient navigation, access to care, communication, remote monitoring and support. Judges evaluated each solution on its technical complexity, potential to scale and novelty. The judges were Dianne Teal, regional chief nursing director at Ochsner Health; Craig Davis, founder and CEO of Catalyze Labs; Trivia Frazier, biotech founder and CEO of Obatala Sciences; and Dr. Patrick Quinlan, founder and CEO of Hippo Technologies and former CEO of Ochsner Health. Ochsner Health brought clinical expertise and leadership to the challenge through Ochsner MD Anderson Cancer Center. "We have so many big problems to solve, and we're not going to solve them by continuing to do what we've always done," Teal said. "Having the fresh eyes of young people on how we're going to solve these things is so critical." The finals also featured remarks from Scott Mabry, chief operating officer of Ochsner Health Capital Region, and Eli Brodsky, deputy director of the Louisiana Department of Health. Brodsky discussed the state's investments to improve healthcare access in rural communities, including a new fund to support companies testing and scaling direct-to-patient technologies in rural Louisiana. Beyond the competition For Reid, DevDays turned into more than a shot at a cash prize. "I'm going to be honest, what got me into this project was the prize money," Reid said. "But hearing from the judges how we can take this from just a pitch, an idea, and really turn it into a business has me thinking way past this competition. We can actually make a real startup. I'm really thankful to Nexus for broadening our horizons and giving us an opportunity to do something we wouldn't have done without them." The team now plans to work toward bringing Tomorrow to market. As DevDays winners, they also automatically advance to the Nexus Technology Cup in December. DevDays is Nexus Louisiana's innovation competition that connects Louisiana college students with industry partners seeking new approaches to real operational and community challenges. Participants build functional solutions, receive expert feedback and present their work to potential employers, partners and investors. The Cancer Care and Prevention Challenge continues a partnership between Nexus Louisiana and Ochsner Health that previously challenged students to improve adolescent ACL injury prevention and recovery.

item.title: Southern University awarded $1.275 million to launch rural business center
item.description: Southern University and A&M College has received a $1.275 million, three-year cooperative agreement from the Minority Business Development Agency (MBDA) to establish the Louisiana Innovation for Thriving Rural Business (LIFT) Center, an initiative designed to strengthen rural businesses, expand access to financing and government contracting opportunities, and increase advanced manufacturing capabilities across Louisiana. Housed in the College of Business, the LIFT Center will provide eligible rural Louisiana businesses with coordinated access to business assessments, consulting, training and specialized assistance. Southern is one of only three historically Black colleges and universities in the country selected by MBDA to lead a Rural Business Center focused on advancing rural and manufacturing-based small businesses. The center will bring together expertise from the Southern University Law Center, the College of Sciences and Engineering, and Southern’s Advanced Metal Additive Manufacturing Laboratory. Through this collaboration, business owners will have access to resources designed to strengthen their operations, prepare for financing, pursue government contracting opportunities and expand their capacity to compete in advanced manufacturing industries. A signature hands-on manufacturing program will give entrepreneurs opportunities to explore businesses focused on making, repairing and testing metal parts for agriculture, energy and defense supply chains. Participants will pair advanced manufacturing expertise with business training to help transform technical skills into viable and sustainable enterprises. KDM & Associates LLC will lead program management and provide consulting in cybersecurity certification readiness, federal contracting, supplier development and manufacturing. Through the LIFT Center, Southern and its partners will work to expand the pool of contract-ready small and emerging businesses positioned to pursue opportunities with federal agencies, including the Small Business Administration, Department of War, Department of Energy, Department of Commerce, NASA, U.S. Department of Agriculture, U.S. Department of Education, Department of Housing and Urban Development, Department of the Interior and Department of Transportation. KDM’s digital platform also will provide virtual training, connect businesses with prospective partners and help monitor participant progress. Over the three-year award period, the LIFT Center aims to serve 500 clients, help 50 new businesses enter the federal supply chain, assist clients in securing $2.125 million in capital and support the creation of 600 jobs. The center will serve eligible rural Louisiana businesses through business assistance, entrepreneurial development and workforce training. These services are designed to expand access to markets, strengthen business capacity and support the long-term growth of Louisiana’s rural economy beyond the award period. Patrick Mensah, Formosa Endowed Professor of Mechanical Engineering and senior associate vice chancellor for academic affairs, will serve as principal investigator. Donald Andrews, professor and dean of the College of Business, will serve as co-principal investigator. Aloyce R. Kaliba, of the College of Business, will serve as project director, and Keith Moore of KDM & Associates will serve as collaborating program manager. Business owners seeking information about eligibility, services and upcoming activities may contact Mensah at patrick.mensah@sus.edu.

item.title: Southern University esports team advances to national HBCU tournament finals; watch party set for Sunday
item.description:
Southern University students will compete for national recognition Sunday, Oct. 4, as the Penny Games championship bracket gets underway, with SU EDGE (esports, development and gaming ecosystem) hosting a campus watch party for students, faculty, staff, alumni and community supporters.  The Penny Games, hosted by the Penny Foundation, brings together 41 top HBCU student competitors competing in College Football 27 and Super Smash Bros. for a share of a $7,600 total prize pool. The Games is designed to prepare young leaders for the evolving digital economy through competitive gaming, critical thinking and exposure to employers and academic institutions. Southern University has emerged as one of the tournament's top-performing programs, with Jaguar competitors securing six of the top eight spots in College Football 27 during initial bracket play. Southern also secured a top-five position in Super Smash Bros. Southern University Tournament Standings College Football 27 — $3,800 prize pool 1st — Jaeveon Jordan (Jordooo2x)
2nd — Coby Robinson (K1ngc0by)
3rd — Ventrice Curtis (retxce)
4th — Derrick Pittman (Trup1tt)
6th — Jeremiah Hollins (Pr33min3ntJayy)
8th — Gavin Miniex (Yeeaaa_gav) Super Smash Bros. — $3,800 prize pool 5th — Timothy Ray (Apxllo) SU EDGE, housed within the College of Sciences and Engineering, continues to expand Southern University's presence in competitive gaming and technology innovation. "The incredible performance of our students in The Penny Games is a testament to the talent, strategic discipline, and dedication within the SU EDGE program," said Christopher Turner, director of SU EDGE. "Esports at Southern University isn't just about gaming—it’s a gateway to STEM pathways, digital leadership, and high-impact career exposure. Seeing our players dominate six of the top eight spots in College Football 27 highlights the competitive excellence that the College of Sciences and Engineering continues to cultivate. We are immensely proud of our student-athletes representing Jaguar Nation on a national level.” Players in College Football 27 are competing for cash prizes of up to $1,500, while Super Smash Bros. players can earn up to $1,400. The championship bracket and finals will stream online Sunday, Oct. 4, beginning at 11 a.m. central time. SU EDGE will host an official campus watch party at the SU EDGE Esports Innovation Lab inside of the Smith-Brown Memorial Student Union, giving the Southern University community an opportunity to watch and support the Jaguar competitors as they compete for tournament titles. The watch party is free and open to students, faculty, staff and the community.  To watch the live broadcast on Sunday, click here.

item.title: CareSouth commits $2.875 million to Southern University’s capital campaign
item.description: CareSouth has committed $2.875 million to Southern University through the Imagine Southern Capital Campaign, providing significant support for scholarships, academic programs, athletics and other initiatives that enhance the student experience across the Southern University System. The announcement was made Wednesday, Sept. 30 at the Valdry Center for Philanthropy at Southern University. “This generous commitment from CareSouth demonstrates what is possible when our community partners invest intentionally in the future of Southern University and our students,” said Orlando McMeans, interim president of the Southern University System. “These resources will impact multiple areas, create opportunities that strengthen the Southern experience for our stakeholders.” CareSouth has partnered with Southern University since 2018, beginning with a co-branding project with Southern University Athletics. Its most recent large gift was a multiyear $1.4M contribution to benefit student scholarships and campus initiatives, including the statewide response to Covid-19 in 2020. This ultimately led to CareSouth establishing free health clinics for students and employees at Southern University’s Baton Rouge and Shreveport campuses. The gift represents a broad commitment to Southern and its mission of access and opportunity, with funding designated for an endowed scholarship fund, Southern University Athletics, the Southern University “Human Jukebox” Marching Band, Southern University School of Nursing, Southern University System Foundation programming, Southern University Alumni Federation and Southern University at Shreveport. “We have seen the value in the relationship with Southern,” said Matthew Valliere, chief executive officer for CareSouth. “When they call, we want to answer that call. I used to be a student here at Southern University, and scholarship opportunities are few and far between. So, for us (CareSouth) to be able to offer that and see the gratitude of the students… the impact that those scholarship dollars make warms my heart.” Sandra Brown, dean of the School of Nursing and Allied Health at Southern University and A&M College, echoed Valliere’s sentiments about the impact of investing in the university and its students. “The power of giving is not found in the check,” said Brown, who is also the vice chancellor for health initiatives at Southern. “The power of giving is found in the lives that are changed because someone chose to give. It means one gift can become a scholarship, one scholarship can become a degree, one degree can become a career, one career can change a family, and one changed family can change a community. That is the ripple effect of generosity.” The commitment advances the goals of the Imagine Southern Capital Campaign, Southern University’s comprehensive investment in the future of the Southern University System and the students, communities, and industries it serves. Grounded in a proud legacy of access, excellence, and opportunity, the campaign is designed to strengthen academic excellence, expand student success, and deepen the University’s impact across Louisiana and beyond. For more about the campaign, go to https://foundation.sus.edu/imagine-southern/.

item.title: Southern University System Presidential Search Committee announces semifinalists
item.description:
The Southern University System Presidential Search Committee today selected semifinalists to advance in the national search for the next president of the Southern University System. The Search Committee selected the following individuals to advance to the semifinalist stage: Brian K. Bridges, Ph.D.
Senior Advisor, Whiteboard Advisors
Former Secretary of Higher Education, State of New Jersey (2020-2025) John K. Belton, J.D.
District Attorney, Third Judicial District Court — Louisiana Jaffus Hardrick, Ed.D.
Former President, Florida Memorial University  Roscoe Jones, J.D.
Former Dean, Drake University Law School  Larissa Littleton-Steib, Ph.D.
Chancellor, Delgado Community College Willie E. Smith, Ed.D.
Chancellor, Baton Rouge Community College “Today represents an important milestone in our search for the next president of the Southern University System,” said Jason Hughes, chair, 2026 Southern University System Presidential Search Committee. “Our committee has approached this responsibility thoughtfully and deliberately, recognizing the significance of selecting the individual who will help lead the nation’s only historically Black university system into its next chapter. We are pleased with the progress of the search and look forward to learning more about each of these candidates as we move into the interview phase.” The selection of semifinalists follows an extensive national search process that has included stakeholder engagement throughout the Southern University System and outreach to prospective candidates. More than 350 students, faculty, staff, administrators, alumni and community stakeholders participated in engagement sessions earlier this year, providing input on the experience, qualities and leadership characteristics desired in the System’s next president. The Search Committee extends its appreciation to TM² Executive Search, which has assisted the Southern University System throughout the national search process. The firm has worked with the committee to facilitate stakeholder engagement, develop the presidential prospectus, conduct candidate outreach and research, and guide the committee through the evaluation and selection process. “The committee is grateful to TM² Executive Search for its guidance and expertise throughout this process,” Hughes said. “Their work, along with the valuable input we received from stakeholders across the Southern University System, has helped us conduct a comprehensive search focused on identifying highly qualified leaders who understand both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with leading this historic System.” Next Steps The semifinalists will be invited to participate in in-person interviews with the Presidential Search Committee in the coming weeks. Following those interviews, the committee will determine which candidates will advance to the finalist stage of the search process. Additional information regarding the interview process and subsequent steps in the presidential search will be announced as details are finalized. The Southern University System launched the national search following the departure of its previous president. The Presidential Search Committee includes representatives from across the Southern University System and the broader community and is charged with recommending finalists for consideration by the Southern University Board of Supervisors. About the Southern University System The Southern University System is the nation’s only historically Black university system and includes Southern University and A&M College, Southern University at New Orleans, Southern University at Shreveport, Southern University Law Center and the Southern University Agricultural Research and Extension Center. Through teaching, research and service, the System is committed to providing educational access and opportunity while developing leaders and strengthening communities throughout Louisiana and beyond.

item.title: Dr. Leroy C. Roquemore Symposium 2026
Southern University System celebrates scholarship support and student success at 2nd annual Southern Celebrates Scholarship Event
item.description: The Southern University System hosted its second annual Southern Celebrates Scholarship Event Wednesday at the Southern University Welcome Center, bringing together more than 300 benefactors, corporate partners and student scholars from across the Southern University System to celebrate the impact of scholarships, mentorship and partnerships on student success. The morning brunch highlighted the contributions of supporters whose generosity provides direct support to students at Southern University campuses in Baton Rouge, New Orleans and Shreveport. The event also gave benefactors and corporate partners an opportunity to engage with student scholars and Southern University administrative and academic leaders. This year’s event also marked Southern University’s 146th year of service to Louisiana and the nation. Southern University is the nation’s only Historically Black College and University system. “Today is about the gratitude we have for our students who excel and raise the bar,” said Dr. Orlando McMeans, interim president of the Southern University System and chancellor of the Southern University Ag Center. “It is equally about gratitude for those who contribute to that excellence — those who give, mentor, provide a network, an ear, or a prayer. We thank you.” The program featured a moderated panel discussion, “The Power of Partnership: Nutrien & Southern University,” facilitated by Alfred E. Harrell III, president and CEO of the Southern University System Foundation. Panelists included Ebonie Raby, senior adviser for community relations and investment at Nutrien; Dr. Robert Easley, director of advancement for the College of Agriculture, Human and Environmental Sciences at Southern University and A&M College; and Bryan Glass, a Southern University student scholar. The discussion highlighted the Nutrien Scholarship Fund at Southern University and explored how sustained corporate-university partnerships can create educational opportunities for students from communities across Louisiana. “Southern’s success is a shared success,” said Harrell. “Every gift, every mentorship, every partnership represented in this room is already at work in the life of a Southern University student. This event is our opportunity to say thank you, and to show our partners exactly what their investment makes possible.” The second annual Southern Celebrates Scholarship Event was made possible through the support of Dow, Mele Printing, Aramark, Renasant Bank, the Southern University System Foundation and the Southern University System. For more information about the Southern University System Foundation and its work supporting donor relations, major gift fundraising, legacy giving and corporate partnerships across the Southern University System, contact Biyaka Williams at biyaka@sutrueblue.org.
